questions.q: A 35-year-old man from rural India presents with a hypopigmented patch on the forearm with loss of sensation and thickened ulnar nerve. Slit skin smear shows acid-fast bacilli. What is the leprosy classification (Ridley-Jopling) that best fits this patient?
questions.exp: BT leprosy presents with a few hypopigmented patches with partial sensory loss and can show thickened peripheral nerves. The presence of AFB on SSS indicates it is not purely TT (which is AFB-negative). BT sits closest to the tuberculoid pole with some bacterial load.

questions.q: A 28-year-old leprosy patient on MDT (PB regimen) develops sudden erythema and edema of existing patches with fever and nerve tenderness. No new lesions appear. The most appropriate immediate management is:
questions.exp: This is a Type 1 lepra reaction (Reversal reaction). Management includes systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone starting at 40 mg/day) while continuing MDT. Thalidomide is used for ENL (Type 2 reaction), not Type 1.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with well-demarcated, scaly, erythematous plaques in the groin and inner thighs. KOH mount shows septate hyphae with arthroconidia. Cultures show flat, powdery colonies with a reddish-brown reverse. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: T. rubrum is the most common cause of tinea cruris. It produces flat, powdery white colonies with a deep wine-red to reddish-brown reverse on SDA. E. floccosum also causes tinea cruris but shows a khaki-yellow colony. Candida shows pseudohyphae on KOH.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with a painless verrucous nodule on the foot that has slowly enlarged over 6 months. Histology shows 'sclerotic bodies' (Medlar bodies) within giant cells. The condition is:
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is characterized histologically by pathognomonic 'Medlar bodies' (sclerotic bodies) - thick-walled, pigmented, septate cells. Mycetoma shows grains. Sporotrichosis is caused by dimorphic fungi without sclerotic bodies.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man with oral mucosal erosions and Nikolsky sign-positive flaccid bullae on the trunk presents for evaluation. DIF of perilesional skin shows IgG and C3 deposits in an intercellular 'fishnet' pattern throughout the epidermis. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris shows intraepidermal blistering with IgG antibodies against desmogleins. DIF shows IgG and C3 in a fishnet/chicken-wire pattern throughout the epidermis. Bullous pemphigoid shows linear IgG at the DEJ.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal and erythematous skin, sparing mucosa. Nikolsky sign is negative. DIF shows linear C3 and IgG along the basement membrane zone. The target antigen is located on:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid targets BP230 and BP180 (BPAG2/type XVII collagen) in the hemidesmosome. BP180 is the main pathogenic target. DIF shows linear IgG/C3 at BMZ. Desmoglein 1 and 3 are targets in pemphigus. Type VII collagen is targeted in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman with a butterfly-shaped erythematous rash on the face, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and arthritis has ANA positive (1:640), anti-dsDNA positive, and low complement. Which skin finding, if present on biopsy, is pathognomonic for this condition?
opts: Positive lupus band test (IgG at DEJ in non-sun-exposed skin)
questions.exp: The lupus band test (LBT) showing immunoglobulin deposits at the DEJ in non-sun-exposed, non-lesional skin is specific for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). It is positive in 50-80% of SLE patients in uninvolved non-sun-exposed skin. Interface dermatitis can occur in many conditions.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with thickening and tightening of the skin of the fingers and forearms, Raynaud's phenomenon, and dysphagia. ANA shows anticentromere pattern. This is most consistent with:
questions.exp: Anticentromere antibodies are associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc/CREST: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias). Diffuse SSc is associated with anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies.

questions.q: A 24-year-old sexually active man presents with a painless, indurated, clean-based ulcer on the glans penis with non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy shows spirochetes. The first-line treatment is:
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
Azithromycin 500 mg once daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (painless chancre with non-tender LN) is treated with Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose. This is the recommended first-line treatment per WHO and CDC guidelines.

questions.q: A 26-year-old woman presents with painful genital ulcers, inguinal bubo, and systemic features. C-reactive protein is elevated. She recently returned from West Africa. Culture grows a Gram-negative coccobacillus on chocolate agar with satellite phenomenon around Staphylococcus colonies. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi) presents with painful genital ulcers and tender suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy. H. ducreyi grows on chocolate agar requiring XV factor and shows satellite phenomenon around S. aureus colonies. LGV is caused by C. trachomatis serovars L1-L3.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with multiple honey-colored crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. The most common causative organism is:
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo (the most common form) is caused predominantly by Staphylococcus aureus in most settings. It presents with honey-colored crusted lesions. S. pyogenes can also cause impetigo but S. aureus is now the predominant pathogen in most countries.

questions.q: A 45-year-old diabetic man presents with rapidly spreading erythema, severe pain, and crepitus on palpation of the scrotum and perineum. CT shows gas in the soft tissues. The most appropriate management is:
opts: Emergency surgical debridement with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy as primary treatment
Incision and drainage with local antibiotics
questions.exp: This is Fournier's gangrene (necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum/scrotum). It is a surgical emergency requiring immediate wide surgical debridement combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. Delay in surgery significantly increases mortality.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the lips, with fever and painful lymphadenopathy. This is the first episode. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Primary HSV-1 infection in children presents as acute herpetic gingivostomatitis with fever, drooling, painful oral vesicles and ulcers, and regional lymphadenopathy. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. Varicella presents with generalized pruritic vesicles.

questions.q: A 70-year-old immunocompromised patient presents with dermatomal pain followed by grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in the thoracic region that has lasted for 2 weeks. The most common serious complication in this age group is:
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most common serious complication of herpes zoster, especially in elderly patients (>60 years). It occurs due to nerve damage from viral infection and results in persistent pain lasting >3 months after rash resolution.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery-white scales on the elbows, knees, and scalp. Auspitz sign is positive. Histology shows parakeratosis, suprapapillary thinning, and Munro microabscesses. The correct diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Psoriasis vulgaris presents with well-demarcated, silvery-scaled plaques. Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on removal of scale) is characteristic. Histology shows Munro microabscesses (neutrophilic collections in stratum corneum), parakeratosis, and regular acanthosis.

questions.q: A psoriasis patient is started on methotrexate. After 2 years of therapy, which investigation is most important to monitor for the most serious cumulative side effect?
questions.exp: Hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis are the most serious cumulative dose-dependent side effects of long-term methotrexate therapy. Liver biopsy is recommended when cumulative dose reaches 1.5 g (some guidelines suggest using fibrosis markers). Regular monitoring of liver enzymes alone is insufficient.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with intensely pruritic vesicles on the extensor surfaces of elbows and knees. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at the tips of dermal papillae. Gut biopsy shows villous atrophy. The best treatment is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with celiac disease. DIF shows pathognomonic granular IgA at dermal papillae tips. Treatment involves dapsone for rapid itch relief and strict gluten-free diet for long-term management (allows reduction/cessation of dapsone).

questions.q: A patient with eczema is started on a topical calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus ointment). Which of the following is an absolute contraindication?
questions.exp: Tacrolimus ointment (Protopic) 0.03% is indicated for patients aged 2 years and above. It is contraindicated in children under 2 years of age. The 0.1% formulation is for adults only. Facial application is actually one of the preferred uses.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with photosensitivity, violaceous discoloration of the eyelids (heliotrope rash), and periungual telangiectasias. Muscle enzymes (CK, LDH) are elevated. The specific antibody most associated with malignancy in this condition is:
questions.exp: In dermatomyositis, anti-TIF1-gamma (anti-p155/140) antibodies are strongly associated with cancer-associated myositis. Anti-Jo-1 is associated with antisynthetase syndrome (interstitial lung disease). Anti-Mi-2 is associated with classic DM with good prognosis. Anti-MDA5 is linked to rapidly progressive ILD.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with recurrent painful aphthous ulcers in the mouth, genital ulcers, pseudofolliculitis, and uveitis. Pathergy test is positive. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Behcet's disease is characterized by recurrent oral and genital ulcers, ocular involvement (uveitis), and skin findings including pseudofolliculitis and erythema nodosum. Positive pathergy test (formation of papule/pustule 24-48h after needle prick) is specific for Behcet's disease.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man with a 20-pack-year smoking history presents with a pearly papule with telangiectasias on the nose, which has been slowly growing for 2 years. It has a central ulcer. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Noduloulcerative BCC presents as a pearly translucent papule/nodule with telangiectasias and rolled borders, with central ulceration ('rodent ulcer'). It is the most common skin cancer. It grows slowly over months to years and occurs predominantly on sun-exposed areas in fair-skinned individuals.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with an irregular, asymmetric, multicolored lesion on the back that has changed in size over 6 months. Dermoscopy shows atypical pigment network, regression structures, and blue-white veil. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is positive. The pathological staging is at minimum:
questions.exp: AJCC staging for melanoma: positive sentinel lymph node biopsy indicates regional nodal metastasis, which is Stage III regardless of primary tumor characteristics. Stage IV requires distant metastases.

questions.q: A patient on long-term phenytoin therapy develops coarsening of facial features, gingival hyperplasia, hypertrichosis, and acneiform lesions. These are examples of:
questions.exp: Gingival hyperplasia, hypertrichosis, coarsening of facial features, and acneiform eruptions from phenytoin are pharmacological (Type A) reactions - predictable, dose-dependent extensions of the drug's mechanism. These are not hypersensitivity reactions.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman develops fever, lymphadenopathy, and a widespread morbilliform rash 3 weeks after starting allopurinol. She has elevated liver enzymes and eosinophilia. The diagnosis is:
opts: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
questions.exp: DRESS (Drug Hypersensitivity Syndrome) presents 2-6 weeks after starting the offending drug with rash, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and internal organ involvement (hepatitis, nephritis). Allopurinol is a common trigger. RegiSCAR score is used for diagnosis.

questions.q: A 14-year-old girl presents with recurrent well-demarcated, erythematous to violaceous, round patches at the same site on the lip every time she takes ibuprofen. On resolution, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation remains. This is:
questions.exp: Fixed drug eruption presents as round or oval, erythematous to dusky plaques that recur at the exact same site with each exposure to the causative drug. NSAIDs (especially oxicams and propionic acid derivatives) are common causes. Residual hyperpigmentation is characteristic.

questions.q: During skin patch testing, a patient shows a reaction at 48 hours that has increased at 96 hours reading. This pattern is most consistent with:
questions.exp: Patch testing detects Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity. Readings at 48 and 96 hours (or 72h + 96/120h) are standard. Reactions that increase or persist from 48h to 96h are characteristic of true allergic contact dermatitis. Declining reactions suggest irritant reactions.

questions.q: A patient undergoes Mohs micrographic surgery for a skin cancer on the nose. Which of the following best describes the advantage of this technique over standard excision?
opts: It destroys the tumor without incision using photosensitizers
It allows 100% margin examination by horizontal frozen sections processed in-stages
It uses lymphatic mapping to detect spread
It reduces risk of recurrence by ensuring negative sentinel lymph nodes
questions.exp: Mohs surgery is tissue-sparing and allows complete (100%) margin assessment using horizontal frozen sections processed in stages while the patient waits. Standard excision examines only ~1% of the margin. It achieves the highest cure rates for high-risk BCCs and SCCs, especially on the face.

questions.q: A patient with vitiligo is undergoing phototherapy. The mechanism by which narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) stimulates repigmentation is primarily through:
opts: Direct melanocyte cytotoxicity followed by repopulation
Stimulation of melanocyte migration from hair follicle outer root sheath reservoirs
Induction of regulatory T cells to suppress melanocyte-directed autoimmunity
Inhibition of IL-15 signaling in keratinocytes
questions.exp: NB-UVB repigmentation in vitiligo occurs primarily through activation and proliferation of melanocyte precursors (melanoblasts) residing in the outer root sheath of hair follicles, which then migrate into the epidermis. This is why repigmentation begins perifollicularly.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with solar lentigines, freckling, and early skin cancers after minimal sun exposure. DNA repair enzyme testing confirms deficiency. She likely has mutations in:
opts: Nucleotide excision repair genes (XP complementation groups)
questions.exp: Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is caused by mutations in nucleotide excision repair (NER) genes (XPA-XPG complementation groups, or XPV). Patients cannot repair UV-induced DNA damage (CPDs, 6-4 photoproducts), leading to extreme photosensitivity and 1000-fold increased risk of skin cancers.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with recurrent skin infections, partial oculocutaneous albinism, peripheral neuropathy, and giant granules in leukocytes on peripheral blood smear. The underlying defect is in:
questions.exp: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by mutations in the LYST gene (lysosomal trafficking regulator). It leads to giant lysosomes/granules in all granule-containing cells, partial albinism, recurrent infections, and peripheral neuropathy. Giant azurophilic granules in neutrophils on PBS are pathognomonic.
